recall_prompt: Say how you would find 3x² + 6x — what you add to both sides, what you compare with, how you find p, q and y, and how the value of 1 + x gives the answer.
insider_note: Add 1 on both sides first — the printed series has no leading 1 to match the expansion. Finish by squaring 1 + x = √(5/3): the 3x² + 6x asked for appears on its own, with no need to solve for x.

steps.label: Rewrite with factorials
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Each denominator is a product like 5·10·15 = 5³·(1·2·3), so every term becomes (a product)/(k!) times (1/5)ᵏ. The series has no leading 1, so add 1 to both sides first; the formula is then written in y because x is already taken.
steps.memory_tip: 5·10·15 = 5³·3!, so each term is (a product)/k! times (1/5)ᵏ. No leading 1 is printed — add 1 to both sides.

recall.must_convey: That the series is rewritten so the k-th term is a product over k! times (1/5) to the power k, after adding 1 on both sides so the missing early terms are present.
accept: write each term as a product over k factorial times one by five to the power k and add 1 on both sides
split each denominator into five to the power k times k factorial
add 1 to both sides and bring the series to the shape one plus p by one factorial into x by q and so on
prathi term ni k factorial tho, one by five power k tho rayali, rendu sides ki 1 add cheyali
rewrite the denominators as powers of five times factorials

steps.why: The standard expansion of (1 − y)^(−p/q) has a k! in every denominator and a fixed ratio y/q raised to k. Until the given series is written in that exact shape, p, q and y cannot be read off.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add 1 on both sides when the series starts late, so the comparison has no 1 to match.
Writing 5·10·15 as 5·3! instead of 5³·3! — every factor carries a 5.
Losing the alternating sign when the terms alternate.

steps.label: Compare with the standard expansion
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for WRITING the standard expansion beside the series. The examiner looks for the pattern p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!. All plus signs mean the (1 − y) form.
steps.memory_tip: All plus signs mean the (1 − y) form. The pattern is p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over the factorials.

recall.must_convey: That the series is compared with the expansion of (1 − y) to the power minus p by q, whose coefficients are p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!.
accept: compare with the expansion of (1 − y) to the power minus p by q
match it with one plus p by one factorial into y by q plus p into p plus q by two factorial into y by q squared and so on
use the standard binomial series with negative fractional index (1 − y) to the power minus p by q
(1 − y)^(−p/q) formula tho compare cheyali
the pattern p then p into p plus q over the factorials is the standard series

steps.why: This is the only binomial expansion whose coefficients grow as p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q). Naming it turns the rest of the question into reading off three numbers.
common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form for an alternating series or the (1 + x) form for an all-plus series.
Writing p(p + 1) instead of p(p + q) — the step between factors is q, not 1.

steps.label: Find p, q and y
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. p is the first factor (1), p + q is the second (3) so q = 2, and y/q equals the common ratio 1/5 so y = q/5 = 2/5.
steps.memory_tip: p = 1, p + q = 3 so q = 2, and y/q = 1/5 gives y = 2/5.

recall.must_convey: That p = 1 and p + q = 3 give q = 2, and y/q = 1/5 gives y = two by five.
accept: p is one, p plus q is three so q is two, and y by q is one by five so y is two by five
the first factor gives p equal to one and the second gives q equal to two
y by q equals one by five so y equals two by five
p one, q two vasthai, y by q one by five kabatti y two by five
read off p from the first numerator and q from the gap between the factors

steps.why: Three unknowns need three matches: the first numerator fixes p, the second fixes p + q, and the ratio inside the bracket fixes y/q. Nothing else in the series is free.
common_mistakes: Taking y = 1/5 directly — the bracket holds y/q, so y = q × 1/5.
Reading q from the second factor as a whole instead of as p + q.

steps.label: Evaluate the power
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Substitute p, q, y into (1 − y)^(−p/q) and simplify the fraction inside the bracket before touching the exponent.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives one plus x equals root of five by three.
accept: substituting gives one plus x equals root of five by three
put the values into (1 − y)^(−p/q) and simplify to get one plus x equals root of five by three
the bracket becomes three by five and the power gives one plus x equals root of five by three
values substitute cheste one plus x equals root of five by three vasthundi
simplify the bracket first then apply the negative index
heard_as: one plus x equals root of five by three

steps.why: A negative index inverts the fraction and a fractional index takes a root. Doing the inversion first keeps the root over a simple fraction.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exponent instead of the fraction when the index is negative.
Leaving a root in the denominator without a clear final value.

steps.label: Square and rearrange
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Square 1 + x = √(5/3), multiply by 3, and the left side is 3 + 6x + 3x². The 3x² + 6x asked for is sitting there.
steps.memory_tip: 3x² + 6x is 3(1 + x)² − 3, so squaring 1 + x is enough. x itself is never needed.

recall.must_convey: That squaring 1 + x = √(5/3) and multiplying by 3 gives 3 + 6x + 3x² = 5, so 3x² + 6x = 2.
accept: square both sides to get one plus x squared is five by three then three x squared plus six x is two
squaring gives three plus six x plus three x squared equals five so the answer is two
three x squared plus six x equals two
square chesi three tho multiply cheste three x squared plus six x is two
the answer is two

steps.why: The question asks for 3x² + 6x, which is 3(1 + x)² − 3. Finding 1 + x as one number is enough; x itself is never needed.
common_mistakes: Solving for x = √(5/3) − 1 and substituting — correct but slow and easy to get wrong.
